claim: Optogenetic excitation of GABAergic neurons produced more effective inactivation than light-gated ion pumps.
source: Optogenetic excitation of GABAergic neurons produced more effective inactivation than light-gated ion pumps.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing ChR-assisted photoinhibition with direct photoinhibition using Arch and Jaws, showing ChR-assisted methods required lower laser powers (0.5-1.5 mW) to achieve >80% spike rate reduction compared to ~10-fold higher power for Arch and Jaws (Figure 1E).

claim: Transgenic mice expressing the light-dependent chloride channel GtACR1 produced the most potent inactivation.
source: Transgenic mice expressing the light-dependent chloride channel GtACR1 produced the most potent inactivation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing GtACR1 produced >80% spike silencing at 0.1 mW, lower than all other methods tested (Figure 2C).

claim: Inactivation spread substantially beyond the photostimulation light, caused by strong coupling between cortical neurons.
source: Generally, inactivation spread substantially beyond the photostimulation light, caused by strong coupling between cortical neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition extended 1 mm beyond the activation profile of FS neurons (Figure 5B) and by observations that both FS and pyramidal neurons decreased activity in regions surrounding photostimulation (Figure 9).

claim: Over some range of light intensity, optogenetic excitation of inhibitory neurons reduced activity in these neurons, together with pyramidal neurons, a signature of inhibition-stabilized neural networks ('paradoxical effect').
source: Over some range of light intensity, optogenetic excitation of inhibitory neurons reduced activity in these neurons, together with pyramidal neurons, a signature of inhibition-stabilized neural networks ('paradoxical effect').
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that FS neurons decreased their activity despite being excited by ReaChR, roughly in proportion with pyramidal neurons (Figure 10B), consistent with predictions from inhibition-stabilized network models.

claim: The offset of optogenetic inactivation was followed by rebound excitation in a light dose-dependent manner, limiting temporal resolution.
source: The offset of optogenetic inactivation was followed by rebound excitation in a light dose-dependent manner, limiting temporal resolution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing removal of photoinhibition elevated spike rate above baseline, with rebound activity depending on both photostimulus duration and intensity (Figure 12A-C).

claim: Blue light is highly confined in cortical tissue with light intensity dropping to less than 20% at 500 µm below the surface of the brain.
source: Light intensity attenuated rapidly as a function of depth, to less than 20% at 500 µm below the surface of the brain (Figure 3D; depth at half max, 300 µm).
evidence: Supported by photobleaching measurements in transgenic mice expressing GFP in nuclei of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3A-D).

claim: Blue light intensity dropped off laterally to 50% at 135 µm from the laser center.
source: Laterally, light intensity dropped off to 50% at 135 µm (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by photobleaching measurements showing spatial profile of blue light (Figure 3D).

claim: Orange light propagated much further than blue light, with depth at half max of 846 µm.
source: In contrast to blue light, orange light propagated much further (depth at half max, 846 µm), penetrating all layers of cortex and illuminating a cubic millimeter of volume (Figure 3E–G), 28 times larger than for blue light.
evidence: Supported by photobleaching measurements in transgenic mice expressing mCherry in nuclei of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 3E-G).

claim: ChR-assisted photoinhibition in transgenic mice produced strong inactivation with >80% reduction in spike rate for putative pyramidal neurons with low laser powers (0.5–1.5 mW).
source: Near the center of the photostimulus (<0.4 mm from laser center), ChR-assisted photoinhibition in transgenic mice produced strong inactivation, with >80% of reduction in spike rate for putative pyramidal neurons with low laser powers (0.5–1.5 mW, Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by silicon probe recordings measuring spike rates during photostimulation in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP, PV-IRES-Cre x Ai32, and other transgenic mice (Figure 1E).

claim: Arch and Jaws-mediated photoinhibition required roughly 10-fold higher laser power to achieve similar silencing compared to ChR-assisted photoinhibition.
source: Arch and Jaws-mediated photoinhibition required roughly 10-fold higher laser power to achieve similar silencing compared to ChR-assisted photoinhibition (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing laser power requirements across different optogenetic methods (Figure 1E).

claim: For Arch-mediated photoinhibition, temporally-modulated photostimuli were more effective in silencing activity than constant photostimuli at the same average power.
source: For Arch-mediated photoinhibition, temporally-modulated photostimuli were more effective in silencing activity than constant photostimuli at the same average power (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing 40 Hz sinusoid photostimulus with constant photostimulus (Figure 1F).

claim: GtACR1 produced the most potent photoinhibition near the laser center, with >80% of spikes silenced at 0.1 mW.
source: Under blue light (473 nm) illumination, GtACR1 produced the most potent photoinhibition near the laser center, with >80% of the spikes silenced at 0.1 mW (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by silicon probe recordings in Emx1-IRES-Cre x GtACR1 mice (Figure 2C).

claim: Below 0.2 mW, photostimulation of soma localized GtACR1 induced little excitation.
source: Below 0.2 mW, photostimulation of soma localized GtACR1 induced little excitation (Mahn et al., 2018; Messier et al., 2018) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate during first 20 ms of photostimulation onset (Figure 2D) and by citations to previous studies.

claim: At higher laser powers, transient short-latency excitation was apparent with GtACR1, which was likely due to axonal excitation.
source: At higher laser powers, transient short-latency excitation was apparent, which was likely due to axonal excitation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing axonal excitation at 0.8 mW laser power (Figure 2D) and inference based on known properties of GtACR1 expression in axons.

claim: Photostimulation of ChR2 in GABAergic neurons produced nearly uniform inhibition of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers.
source: Photostimulation of ChR2 in GABAergic neurons produced nearly uniform inhibition of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers (Figure 4A, VGAT-ChR2-EYFP, Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32, and PV-IRES-Cre X Ai32), despite limited penetration of blue light in tissue (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by silicon probe recordings showing relative spike rate across cortical depth (Figure 4A) and comparison with light penetration data (Figure 3).

claim: Photoinhibition removed the majority of spikes (>80%) in a column across a wide range of laser powers (1.5–14 mW).
source: Photoinhibition removed the majority of spikes (>80%) in a column across a wide range of laser powers (1.5–14 mW), indicating that photoinhibition is an effective method for local inactivation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate across cortical layers at different laser powers (Figure 4A-B).

claim: At low laser powers (0.5 mW) in Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice, selective excitation of Sst neurons produced a disinhibition of excitatory neurons around layer 4.
source: A notable exception was seen at low laser powers (0.5 mW) in Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice. Selective excitation of Sst neurons produced a disinhibition of excitatory neurons around layer 4 (Figure 4A, , Sst-IRES-Cre X Ai32).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased relative spike rate in layer 4 at 0.5 mW (Figure 4A) and inference based on known circuit connectivity.

claim: This disinhibition in layer four was likely mediated by Sst neurons that inhibit PV neurons.
source: This disinhibition in layer four was likely mediated by Sst neurons that inhibit PV neurons. Activation of Sst neurons therefore removed a major source of inhibition onto excitatory neurons (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on known circuit connectivity supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Despite different propagation of blue and orange light in tissue, ChR-assisted photoinhibition was remarkably similar for both illumination wavelengths.
source: Despite different propagation of blue and orange light in tissue (Figure 3), ChR-assisted photoinhibition was remarkably similar for both illumination wavelengths.
evidence: Supported by comparison of photoinhibition profiles for blue light (Figure 4A) and orange light (Figure 4B) and light propagation data (Figure 3).

claim: At moderate laser power (1.5 mW), blue light excited FS neurons mainly in superficial layers.
source: At moderate laser power (1.5 mW), blue light excited FS neurons mainly in superficial layers (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate of FS neurons across cortical depth (Figure 4C).

claim: Loss of activity was present in both superficial and deep layers despite FS neurons being excited mainly in superficial layers.
source: Yet, loss of activity was present in both superficial and deep layers (see Discussion).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition across all cortical layers (Figure 4A) despite limited FS neuron excitation in deep layers (Figure 4C).

claim: The profile of silencing mediated by GtACR1 was similar for blue and red light, despite profound wavelength-dependent differences of light propagation in tissue.
source: Remarkably, the profile of silencing mediated by GtACR1 was also similar for blue and red light (Figure 4D–E), despite profound wavelength-dependent differences of light propagation in tissue (and much higher power levels required at the longer excitation wavelength).
evidence: Supported by comparison of photoinhibition profiles for blue light (Figure 4D) and red light (Figure 4E) and light propagation data (Figure 3).

claim: In VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, FS neurons near the laser center were activated in a dose-dependent manner.
source: In VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, FS neurons near the laser center were activated in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate of FS neurons as a function of laser power (Figure 5B).

claim: The lateral spread of FS neuron excitation was dependent on laser power (at 0.5 mW, half-max width, 0.15 mm; at 14 mW, 1.5 mm).
source: The lateral spread of FS neuron excitation was dependent on laser power (at 0.5 mW, half-max width, 0.15 mm; at 14 mW, 1.5 mm, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate versus lateral distance for FS neurons at different laser powers (Figure 5B).

claim: A long tail in the light intensity profile can activate light gated channel more than 1 mm from the center of the laser, even for blue excitation light.
source: These measurements show that a long tail in the light intensity profile can activate light gated channel more than 1 mm from the center of the laser, even for blue excitation light.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing FS neuron excitation extending to 1.5 mm at high laser powers (Figure 5B).

claim: Photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons extended 1 mm beyond the activation profile of FS neurons.
source: Photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons extended 1 mm beyond the activation profile of FS neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing pyramidal neuron activity was reduced even 1 mm away from the laser center where FS neurons were not activated (Figure 5B).

claim: This spread of photoinhibition extends beyond typical sizes of dendritic and axonal arbors of GABAergic neurons and dendritic arbors of pyramidal neurons.
source: This spread of photoinhibition extends beyond typical sizes of dendritic and axonal arbors of GABAergic neurons (Jiang et al., 2015) and dendritic arbors of pyramidal neurons (Oberlaender et al., 2012; Oswald et al., 2013; Shepherd et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on comparison of measured photoinhibition spread with known anatomical dimensions from cited literature.

claim: Selectively photostimulating PV neurons produced similarly broad photoinhibition profile as photostimulating all GABAergic neurons.
source: However, a similarly broad photoinhibition profile was induced in PV-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing photoinhibition profiles in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (Figure 5B) and PV-IRES-Cre X Ai32 mice (Figure 5C).

claim: Using orange light to illuminate a larger cortical volume in transgenic mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons produced similar photoinhibition profile to photostimulating ChR2 in PV neurons using blue light.
source: We next sought to produce a broader photoinhibition by using orange light to illuminate a larger cortical volume in transgenic mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons. However, the resulting photoinhibition profile was similar to those produced by photostimulating ChR2 in PV neurons using blue light (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing photoinhibition profiles for ChR2 with blue light (Figure 5C) and ReaChR with orange light (Figure 5D).

claim: Photoinhibition by selective excitation of Sst neurons induced similarly broad photoinhibition.
source: First, photoinhibition by selective excitation of Sst neurons induced similarly broad photoinhibition (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition profile in Sst-IRES-Cre x Ai32 mice (Figure 5E).

claim: Direct photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons using light-gated ion pumps induced similarly broad photoinhibition.
source: Next, direct photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons using light-gated ion pumps (Emx1-IRES-Cre X Ai35D mice or Emx1-IRES-Cre X Camk2a-tTA X Ai79 mice) induced similarly broad photoinhibition (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition profiles for Arch (Figure 5F) and Jaws (Figure 5G).

claim: ChR-assisted photoinhibition in anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) produced similarly broad spatial spread regardless of the method used to drive photoinhibition.
source: ChR-assisted photoinhibition in a different brain region (anterior lateral motor cortex, ALM) also produced similarly broad spatial spread regardless of the method used to drive photoinhibition (Figure 5H–I, blue light photostimulation in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, or orange light photostimulation in PV-IRES-Cre X ReaChR mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition profiles in ALM for VGAT-ChR2-EYFP (Figure 5H) and PV-IRES-Cre X ReaChR (Figure 5I).

claim: Across all methods, the fractional reduction in spike rate near the laser center approximately predicted the lateral spread of photoinhibition.
source: Across all methods, the fractional reduction in spike rate near the laser center approximately predicted the lateral spread of photoinhibition (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relationship between photoinhibition strength and spatial spread across multiple methods (Figure 5J).

claim: The spatial spread of direct photoinhibition induced by GtACR1 was smaller than that produced by other photoinhibition methods.
source: We tested the spatial spread of direct photoinhibition induced by GtACR1. In three different cortical regions, GtACR1-mediated photoinhibition also produced broad photoinhibition (Figure 6A), but the spatial spread was smaller than that produced by other photoinhibition methods (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing spatial spread of GtACR1-mediated photoinhibition (Figure 6A-B) with other methods (Figure 5J).

claim: At 90% spike rate reduction near the laser center, the half-max radius of photoinhibition was 0.8 mm for GtACR1, compared to >1 mm for other methods.
source: For example, at 90% spike rate reduction near the laser center, the half-max radius of photoinhibition was 0.8 mm, compared to >1 mm for other methods (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition strength versus spatial spread for GtACR1 compared to other methods (Figure 6B).

claim: Local infection with Cre-dependent, ChR2-expressing virus in PV-IRES-Cre mice produced the smallest lateral spread in photoinhibition (radius, approximately 0.5 mm).
source: To limit activation of interneurons we injected small volumes of Cre-dependent ChR2 virus in PV-IRES-Cre mice (Cardin et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2012; Lien and Scanziani, 2013; Pafundo et al., 2016). The virus injection localized the expression of ChR2 (diameter of expression, 500 µm, Figure 7A). Silicon probe recordings (Figure 7B) confirmed that photostimulation excited FS neurons only at the infection site (Figure 7C). In the surrounding regions, FS neuron spike rates were even slightly suppressed (e.g. Figure 7C, at 400 µm away). Photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons extended additional several hundred micrometers, with neurons suppressed even 800 µm away from the photostimulus center. At 90% spike rate reduction at the infection site, the half-max radius of photoinhibition was approximately 0.5 mm (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing spatial profile of photoinhibition with virus injection (Figure 7A-D).

claim: Limiting the spatial extend of interneuron excitation reduced photoinhibition spread.
source: Thus, limiting the spatial extend of interneuron excitation reduced photoinhibition spread.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of photoinhibition spread with virus injection (Figure 7D) versus transgenic expression (Figure 5J).

claim: Optogenetic inactivation methods have a fundamental resolution on the order of 1 mm.
source: Overall these results suggest that optgogenetic inactivation methods have a fundamental resolution on the order of 1 mm (Figure 8).
evidence: Inference based on summary of spatial spread measurements across all methods (Figure 8).

claim: In regions surrounding the photostimulation site, a concurrent decrease in activity was observed in both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons, even with ChR-assisted photoinhibition.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, in regions surrounding the photostimulation site, a concurrent decrease in activity was observed in both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons, even with ChR-assisted photoinhibition (Figure 9, arrows).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate versus lateral distance for both FS and pyramidal neurons (Figure 9).

claim: Activity decreased in proportion in FS and pyramidal neurons relative to their baseline activity.
source: Activity decreased in proportion in FS and pyramidal neurons relative to their baseline activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing parallel decreases in relative spike rate for FS and pyramidal neurons in the surround (Figure 9).

claim: Inhibition-stabilized networks exhibit paradoxical effects where selective excitation of interneurons paradoxically decreases interneuron activity together with excitatory neurons.
source: These inhibition-stabilized networks (ISN) exhibit paradoxical effects. Selective excitation of interneurons paradoxically decreases interneuron activity together with excitatory neurons (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2016; Pehlevan and Sompolinsky, 2014; Rubin et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2017; Tsodyks et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical studies of inhibition-stabilized networks.

claim: Because of recurrent excitatory connectivity in cortical circuits, the effects on excitatory neuron spike rates are amplified, which causes a large reduction in excitation of inhibitory interneurons.
source: Because of recurrent excitatory connectivity in cortical circuits, the effects on excitatory neuron spike rates are amplified, which causes a large reduction in excitation of inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: Inference based on known properties of inhibition-stabilized networks and recurrent connectivity.

claim: In mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons, using orange light to illuminate a large part of the cortex, pyramidal neurons monotonically decreased their activity as a function of light intensity.
source: In mice expressing ReaChR in PV neurons, we used orange light to illuminate a large part of the cortex (2 mm beam diameter at 4σ at the surface of the brain) to drive excitation in nearly all PV neurons across cortical layers (Figure 10A). Pyramidal neurons monotonically decreased their activity as a function of light intensity (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of light intensity for pyramidal neurons (Figure 10B).

claim: FS neurons also decreased their activity, roughly in proportion despite being excited by ReaChR.
source: Interestingly, FS neurons also decreased their activity, roughly in proportion despite being excited by ReaChR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of light intensity for FS neurons (Figure 10B).

claim: As a function of light intensity, activity in FS neurons continued to decrease until most of the pyramidal neuron activity was silenced (at 0.4 mW/mm2).
source: As a function of light intensity, activity in FS neurons continued to decrease until most of the pyramidal neuron activity was silenced (Figure 10B, at 0.4 mW/mm2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of light intensity (Figure 10B).

claim: At higher light intensities the FS neuron activity increased, likely driven by an increased photocurrent and transition to a regime with little coupling due to lack of excitatory activity.
source: At higher light intensities the FS neuron activity increased. This increase was likely driven by an increased photocurrent. In addition, the network also transitioned to a regime with little coupling due to lack of excitatory activity.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing FS neuron activity increase at high light intensities (Figure 10B) and understanding of network dynamics.

claim: The data are consistent with the paradoxical effect predicted by cortical circuit models stabilized by inhibition.
source: These data are consistent with the paradoxical effect predicted by cortical circuit models stabilized by inhibition (Tsodyks et al., 1997).
evidence: Inference based on comparison of experimental data (Figure 10) with predictions from cited theoretical models.

claim: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the kinetics of ChR determined the dynamics of the interneurons.
source: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the kinetics of ChR determined the dynamics of the interneurons (Figure 11A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing different temporal dynamics for ChR2 versus ReaChR in FS neurons (Figure 11A).

claim: In mice expressing ChR2 (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP), FS neuron activity was time-locked to the photostimulus.
source: For example, in mice expressing ChR2 (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP), FS neuron activity was time-locked to the photostimulus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH of FS neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (Figure 11A).

claim: In mice expressing ReaChR (PV-IRES-Cre x ReaChR), which has slower off kinetics compared to ChR2, FS neuron activity was not time-locked to the photostimulus and was strongly attenuated over prolonged photostimulation.
source: In mice expressing ReaChR (PV-IRES-Cre x ReaChR), which has slower off kinetics compared to ChR2 (Lin et al., 2012), FS neuron activity was not time-locked to the photostimulus and was strongly attenuated over prolonged photostimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH of FS neurons in PV-IRES-Cre x ReaChR mice (Figure 11A) and citation to Lin et al., 2012 regarding ReaChR kinetics.

claim: Despite the different interneuron dynamics, the photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons was similar.
source: Despite the different interneuron dynamics, the photoinhibition of pyramidal neurons was similarly (Figure 11A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing similar PSTH of pyramidal neurons for ChR2 and ReaChR (Figure 11A).

claim: Prolonged photostimulation (>20 ms) triggered spikes in a subset of FS interneurons, which in turn reduced activity in other FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
source: These data suggest that prolonged photostimulation (>20 ms) triggered spikes in a subset of FS interneurons, which in turn reduced activity in other FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing spike rate changes in FS neurons at different epochs (Figure 11B).

claim: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the photoinhibition lagged FS neuron excitation by 3 ms.
source: For ChR-assisted photoinhibition, the photoinhibition lagged FS neuron excitation by 3 ms (Materials and methods; at >1.5 mW, FS excitation onset, 1.1 ± 0.2 ms).
evidence: Supported by analysis of PSTH data showing timing of FS excitation and pyramidal neuron inhibition.

claim: Photoinhibition was detectable 4.0 ± 1.7 ms after photostimulation onset and reached a maximum at 18.4 ± 1.6 ms ('photoinhibition onset').
source: Photoinhibition was detectable 4.0 ± 1.7 ms after photostimulation onset (mean ± s.e.m., based on t-test of spike counts against baseline) and reached a maximum at 18.4 ± 1.6 ms ('photoinhibition onset', Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of PSTH data (Figure 11C).

claim: ChR2-assisted photoinhibition has a slightly faster onset (14.6 ms) than ReachR-assisted photoinhibition (18.8 ms).
source: ChR2-assisted photoinhibition has a slightly faster onset (14.6 ms) than ReachR-assisted photoinhibition (18.8 ms; p<0.001, bootstrap, one-tailed test, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of photoinhibition onset times (Figure 11C).

claim: Direct hyperpolarization of pyramidal neurons using Arch produced even more rapid photoinhibition onset (5 ms).
source: Direct hyperpolarization of pyramidal neurons using Arch produced even more rapid photoinhibition onset (5 ms, Figure 11C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of photoinhibition onset times for Arch (Figure 11C).

claim: Photoinhibition onset was progressively delayed at increasing distance from the laser center.
source: Photoinhibition onset was progressively delayed at increasing distance from the laser center (Figure 11D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH at different distances from photostimulus center (Figure 11E).

claim: Photoinhibition at 2 mm away lagged the photoinhibition at the laser center by 10 ms.
source: Photoinhibition at 2 mm away lagged the photoinhibition at the laser center by 10 ms (Figure 11E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing photoinhibition onset latencies at different distances (Figure 11E).

claim: This suggests a gradual spread of photoinhibition, consistent with the interpretation that coupling between cortical neurons mediated the photoinhibition spatial spread.
source: This suggests a gradual spread of photoinhibition, consistent with the interpretation that coupling between cortical neurons mediated the photoinhibition spatial spread.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing progressive delay in photoinhibition onset with distance (Figure 11E).

claim: Removal of photoinhibition elevated spike rate above baseline ('rebound activity'), which decayed to baseline over hundreds of milliseconds.
source: The temporal profile of photoinhibition offset was limited by rebound activity. Removal of photoinhibition elevated spike rate above baseline ('rebound activity'), which decayed to baseline over hundreds of milliseconds (Figure 12A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing PSTH after photostimulation offset (Figure 12A).

claim: Rebound activity depended on both photostimulus duration and intensity.
source: Rebound activity depended on both photostimulus duration and intensity (Figure 12B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing spike rates before, during, and after photostimulation for different durations and powers (Figure 12B).

claim: For short photostimulation durations, rebound activity was moderate regardless of photostimulus intensity (at 500 ms duration, rebound activity was 10% of baseline for 1.5–7 mW).
source: For short photostimulation durations, rebound activity was moderate regardless of photostimulus intensity (Figure 12C, e.g. at 500 ms duration, rebound activity was 10% of baseline for 1.5–7 mW).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rebound activity as a function of laser power and photostimulation duration (Figure 12C).

claim: For long photostimulation durations, rebound activity was substantial even at low laser power (following a 4 s duration, rebound spike rate was >30% of baseline spike rate even at 1.5 mW).
source: For long photostimulation durations, rebound activity was substantial even at low laser power (Figure 12C, e.g. following a 4 s duration, rebound spike rate was >30% of baseline spike rate even at 1.5 mW).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rebound activity as a function of laser power and photostimulation duration (Figure 12C).

claim: At moderate photostimulation duration (1 s), all photoinhibition methods produced some rebound activity regardless of photoinhibition strength.
source: At moderate photostimulation duration (1 s), all photoinhibition methods produced some rebound activity regardless of photoinhibition strength (Figure 12D, Pearson's correlation, r = −0.2, p=0.29).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rebound activity as a function of photoinhibition strength across different methods (Figure 12D).

claim: The rebound activity could be caused by recovery from synaptic depression in silenced excitatory neurons, synaptic depression in activated FS neurons, or perturbed intracellular ion concentrations accumulated over prolonged duration of photostimulation.
source: The rebound activity could be caused by recovery from synaptic depression in silenced excitatory neurons, synaptic depression in activated FS neurons, or perturbed intracellular ion concentrations accumulated over prolonged duration of photostimulation (Mahn et al., 2016; Wiegert et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Photoinhibition onset was rapid (10 ms), but the offset was limited by rebound activity.
source: In summary, photoinhibition onset was rapid (10 ms), but the offset was limited by rebound activity.
evidence: Summary inference based on experimental data showing photoinhibition onset (Figure 11C) and rebound activity (Figure 12).

claim: Attenuating the photostimulus gradually (100 ms) or reducing the photostimulus durations can both reduce rebound activity.
source: Attenuating the photostimulus gradually (100 ms) or reducing the photostimulus durations can both reduce rebound activity (Figure 12).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing relationship between photostimulus parameters and rebound activity (Figure 12).

claim: The spatial resolution of optogenetic silencing is approximately one millimeter, with silencing spreading further than the photostimulation light.
source: We found that the spatial resolution of optogenetic silencing is approximately one millimeter, with silencing spreading further than the photostimulation light.
evidence: Summary inference based on experimental data showing spatial spread of photoinhibition across multiple methods (Figures 5-8).

claim: The length scale of photoinhibition is caused by strong coupling within cortical circuits: loss of activity in a focal region withdraws input to other layers and surrounding regions, resulting in loss of activity in both excitatory and inhibitory populations in the surround.
source: The length scale of photoinhibition is caused by strong coupling within cortical circuits: loss of activity in a focal region withdraws input to other layers and surrounding regions, resulting in loss of activity in both excitatory and inhibitory populations in the surround, as predicted by network models (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2016; Rubin et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2017; Tsodyks et al., 1997).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing concurrent decrease in FS and pyramidal neurons in surround (Figure 9) and citations to theoretical models.

claim: At moderate laser powers (1.5 mW) photoinhibition in ChR2-EYFP mice was limited to cortex, with no obvious silencing in subcortical regions immediately below cortex.
source: Consistent with this intensity distribution, at moderate laser powers (1.5 mW) photoinhibition in ChR2-EYFP mice was limited to cortex, with no obvious silencing in subcortical regions immediately below cortex (Guo et al., 2014b).
evidence: Inference based on light intensity distribution (Figure 3) and citation to previous study.

claim: Higher light intensities in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice can cause photoinhibition in the hippocampus and striatum beneath cortical photostimulation sites.
source: However, higher light intensities in these mice can cause photoinhibition in the hippocampus and striatum beneath cortical photostimulation sites (Babl et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Babl et al., 2019.

claim: Silencing mediated by red light is more likely to cause wide-spread direct optogenetic effects compared to blue light, since red light penetrates deeper into the tissue.
source: Silencing mediated by red light is more likely to cause wide-spread direct optogenetic effects compared to blue light, since red light penetrates deeper into the tissue (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on light penetration data (Figure 3) and citation to Lin et al., 2013.

claim: Local expression of ChR limited the excitation of FS interneurons to a small region (~200 um in radius).
source: Local expression of ChR limited the excitation of FS interneurons to a small region (~200 um in radius, Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing FS neuron excitation profile with virus injection (Figure 7C).

claim: In regions surrounding the viral injection site, photostimulation caused a decrease in activity of both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
source: For example, in regions surrounding the viral injection site, photostimulation caused a decrease in activity of both FS neurons and pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing FS neuron spike rates were slightly suppressed at 400 µm away from injection site (Figure 7C).

claim: Similar withdrawal of input could potentially explain the uniform photoinhibition across layers.
source: Similar withdrawal of input could potentially explain the uniform photoinhibition across layers (Hooks et al., 2011; Kiritani et al., 2012), particularly for blue light mediated ChR-assisted photoinhibition (Figure 4A).
evidence: Speculation about mechanism supported by citations and reference to experimental data (Figure 4A).

claim: Given the limited penetration of blue light in tissue at moderate laser powers (1.5 mW), the direct effects of photostimulation on neurons were most pronounced in L2/3, yet pronounced photoinhibition was observed in deep layers.
source: Given the limited penetration of blue light in tissue at moderate laser powers (1.5 mW), the direct effects of photostimulation on neurons were most pronounced in L2/3 (Figure 4C), yet pronounced photoinhibition was observed in deep layers.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of light penetration (Figure 3), FS neuron excitation (Figure 4C), and pyramidal neuron inhibition (Figure 4A) across layers.

claim: In both sensory and motor cortex, cortical neurons cannot maintain activity without thalamic drive.
source: In both sensory and motor cortex, cortical neurons cannot maintain activity without thalamic drive (Guo et al., 2017; Poulet et al., 2012; Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Silencing activity in cortex reduces activity in the thalamus.
source: Conversely, silencing activity in cortex reduces activity in the thalamus (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2017.

claim: Silencing a region in cortex likely decreased activity in the parts of thalamus targeted by the silenced region.
source: Therefore, silencing a region in cortex likely decreased activity in the parts of thalamus targeted by the silenced region.
evidence: Inference based on known corticothalamic connectivity and cited literature.

claim: The data imply that intracortical connections might also be required to maintain cortical activity, in addition to thalamocortical input.
source: Since corticothalamic projections arise from the deep layers, and the direct effects of photostimulation is the strongest in superficial layers (particularly with blue light), our data imply that intracortical connections might also be required to maintain cortical activity, in addition to thalamocortical input.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of layer-specific effects of photostimulation with known anatomy of corticothalamic projections.

claim: Over some range of photostimulus intensities, excitation of interneurons induced the 'paradoxical effect', where activity decreased in both interneurons and excitatory neurons.
source: Our data provide additional evidence for strong coupling between cortical neurons. Over some range of photostimulus intensities, excitation of interneurons induced the 'paradoxical effect', where activity decreased in both interneurons and excitatory neurons (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing concurrent decrease in FS and pyramidal neuron activity during PV neuron photostimulation (Figure 10).

claim: At the center of the laser, weak photostimulation (0.5 mW) of GABAergic neurons induced little increase or even a decrease in FS neurons activity, yet, pyramidal neuron activity was silenced.
source: For example, at the center of the laser, weak photostimulation (0.5 mW) of GABAergic neurons induced little increase or even a decrease in FS neurons activity, yet, pyramidal neuron activity was silenced (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rates at low laser power (Figure 9B).

claim: These observations are consistent with predictions of inhibition-stabilized networks, and they suggest that cortical neurons operate in a regime with strong coupling.
source: These observations are consistent with predictions of inhibition-stabilized networks, and they suggest that cortical neurons operate in a regime with strong coupling (Kato et al., 2017; Lefort et al., 2009; Ozeki et al., 2009; Pehlevan and Sompolinsky, 2014; Rubin et al., 2015; Tsodyks et al., 1997; Sanzeni, 2019).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and citations to theoretical models.

claim: Previous studies manipulated cortical interneurons but did not find the paradoxical effect predicted by inhibition-stabilized network models.
source: Previous studies manipulated cortical interneurons but did not find the paradoxical effect predicted by inhibition-stabilized network models (Atallah et al., 2012; Gutnisky et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One key difference is that we weakly photostimulated nearly all PV neurons in superficial layers of transgenic mice.
source: One key difference is that we weakly photostimulated nearly all PV neurons in superficial layers of transgenic mice.
evidence: Description of experimental approach used in this study.

claim: Previous studies used viral expression strategies that manipulated only subsets of PV neurons.
source: Previous studies used viral expression strategies that manipulated only subsets of PV neurons.
evidence: Comparison with previous studies based on knowledge of their methods.

claim: Theoretical analysis and simulations suggest that the paradoxical effect is only induced when a large proportion of interneurons is excited.
source: Theoretical analysis and simulations suggest that the paradoxical effect is only induced when a large proportion of interneurons is excited (Gutnisky et al., 2017; Sadeh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Cortical networks escape the paradoxical effect regime when most of the pyramidal neurons are silenced.
source: Cortical networks escape the paradoxical effect regime when most of the pyramidal neurons are silenced (Figure 10B), which effectively removes coupling between excitatory neurons.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing FS neuron activity increase at high light intensities (Figure 10B).

claim: The paradoxical effect was only observed under weak photostimulation conditions that do not silence a majority of pyramidal neurons.
source: Consistent with this prediction, the paradoxical effect was only observed under weak photostimulation conditions that do not silence a majority of pyramidal neurons (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing paradoxical effect at low light intensities (Figure 10).

claim: All the data here were collected under awake non-behaving conditions, but previous studies found little difference in photoinhibition strength across behavioral conditions.
source: All the data here were collected under awake non-behaving conditions, but our previous studies found little difference in photoinhibition strength across behavioral conditions (Guo et al., 2014b; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of experimental conditions and citation to previous studies.

claim: ChR-assisted photoinhibition and Cl- channel mediated directed photoinhibition are highly sensitive, producing similarly complete silencing near the laser center across a large range of laser powers (photoinhibition, 1.5–10 mW).
source: ChR-assisted photoinhibition and Cl- channel mediated directed photoinhibition are highly sensitive, producing similarly complete silencing near the laser center across a large range of laser powers (photoinhibition, 1.5–10 mW, Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relative spike rate as a function of laser power (Figure 1E).

claim: The spatial spread of photoinhibition differed substantially across laser powers.
source: However, we note that the spatial spread of photoinhibition differed substantially across laser powers (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing spatial spread as a function of laser power (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: Higher laser power removed spikes over a larger cortical region.
source: Higher laser power removed spikes over a larger cortical region.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing spatial spread increases with laser power (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: This power-dependent spatial spread produces graded loss-of-function manipulations in vivo.
source: This power-dependent spatial spread produces graded loss-of-function manipulations in vivo.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing power-dependent spatial spread.

claim: Photoinhibiting the barrel cortex induced increasingly larger behavioral effects with increasing laser power across a large power range (1.5–10 mW).
source: For example, photoinhibiting the barrel cortex induced increasingly larger behavioral effects with increasing laser power across a large power range (1.5–10 mW) (Guo et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous behavioral study.

claim: In the neocortex, the 1 mm length scale of photoinhibition poses a limit on the spatial resolution of loss-of-function manipulations.
source: In the neocortex, the 1 mm length scale of photoinhibition poses a limit on the spatial resolution of loss-of-function manipulations.
evidence: Inference based on summary of spatial spread measurements (Figure 8).

claim: Interpretation of photoinhibition effects must take this spatial spread function into account.
source: Interpretation of photoinhibition effects must take this spatial spread function into account.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings about spatial spread.

claim: Silencing a brain region nearby to an involved region could produce false-positive behavioral effects.
source: For example, silencing a brain region nearby to an involved region could produce false-positive behavioral effects.
evidence: Inference based on understanding of spatial spread of photoinhibition.

claim: One work-around could involve systematically mapping the photoinhibition effects around a region of interest, then deconvolve the known spatial spread function to recover the underlying region involved in behavior.
source: One work-around could involve systematically mapping the photoinhibition effects (e.g. a behavioral effect) around a region of interest, then deconvolve the known spatial spread function to recover the underlying region involved in behavior (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation about experimental approach supported by citation to previous study.

claim: It is possible that sub-millimeter resolution of photoinhibition could be achieved with direct photoinhibition using more sensitive optogenetic effectors and spatially patterned illuminations.
source: It is possible that sub-millimeter resolution of photoinhibition could be achieved with direct photoinhibition using more sensitive optogenetic effectors and spatially patterned illuminations.
evidence: Speculation about future possibilities.

claim: The spatial resolution of photoinhibition could differ across brain regions.
source: In addition, the spatial resolution of photoinhibition could differ across brain regions.
evidence: Speculation based on understanding of circuit differences across brain regions.

claim: In many subcortical regions GABAergic neurons make long-range projections, reducing the spatial resolution of ChR2-assisted photoinhibition.
source: In many subcortical regions GABAergic neurons make long-range projections, reducing the spatial resolution of ChR2-assisted photoinhibition.
evidence: Inference based on known anatomy of subcortical GABAergic neurons.

claim: Recurrent and lateral excitation is less pronounced in many subcortical regions compared to neocortex, promising better spatial resolution when direct photoinhibition is used for photoinhibition.
source: On the other hand, recurrent and lateral excitation is less pronounced in many subcortical regions compared to neocortex, promising better spatial resolution when direct photoinhibition is used for photoinhibition.
evidence: Inference based on known differences in circuit architecture between cortex and subcortical regions.

claim: The temporal resolution of photoinhibition is limited by rebound activity.
source: Our results suggest that the temporal resolution of photoinhibition is limited by rebound activity (Figure 12), which could potentially produce confounding behavioral consequences.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing rebound activity (Figure 12).

claim: Rebound activity could be partially alleviated by changes in photostimulus parameters.
source: Rebound activity could be partially alleviated by changes in photostimulus parameters (Figure 12C) (Wiegert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing relationship between photostimulus parameters and rebound activity (Figure 12C) and citation.

claim: In many experiments, cell-type-specific manipulations produced multi-phasic network responses both on local and downstream circuits over hundreds of milliseconds.
source: In many experiments, cell-type-specific manipulations produced multi-phasic network responses both on local and downstream circuits over hundreds of milliseconds (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Optogenetic circuit manipulations provide the most insights into functions of specific neural dynamics when the primary effects of the perturbation and the effects on downstream brain areas are taken into account, ideally measured simultaneously in behaving animals.
source: These results highlight that optogenetic circuit manipulations provide the most insights into functions of specific neural dynamics when the primary effects of the perturbation and, equally importantly, the effects on downstream brain areas are taken into account, ideally measured simultaneously in behaving animals (Gao et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2017; Inagaki et al., 2019; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference about best practices supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cerebral cortex consists of dozens of distinct areas.
source: The cerebral cortex consists of dozens of distinct areas (Dong, 2008; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Paxinos and Watson, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical references.

claim: Each brain region in turn contains multiple cell types.
source: Each brain region in turn contains multiple cell types (Rudy et al., 2011; Tasic et al., 2018; Zeng and Sanes, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to cell type classification studies.

claim: Much of what we know about localization of cortical function comes from loss-of-function studies.
source: Much of what we know about localization of cortical function comes from loss-of-function studies.
evidence: General statement about the field based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Classically, lesions, pharmacological inactivation, or cooling have been used to silence activity in small (>1 mm3) regions of tissue.
source: Classically, lesions (Lashley, 1931; Mishkin and Ungerleider, 1982; Newsome and Wurtz, 1988), pharmacological inactivation (Guo et al., 2017; Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Krupa et al., 1999), or cooling (Long and Fee, 2008; Ponce et al., 2008) have been used to silence activity in small (>1 mm3) regions of tissue.
evidence: Supported by citations to classical studies.

claim: The development of optogenetics has allowed rapid and reversible silencing of neuronal activity.
source: The development of optogenetics has allowed rapid and reversible silencing of neuronal activity (Deisseroth, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of optogenetics.

claim: There has been significant progress in creating genetic access to specific neuronal populations.
source: Concurrently, there has been significant progress in creating genetic access to specific neuronal populations (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review of genetic tools.

claim: Various transgenic Cre driver mouse lines target subtypes of cortical neurons.
source: Various transgenic Cre driver mouse lines target subtypes of cortical neurons (Gerfen et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2007; Harris et al., 2014; Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing Cre driver lines.

claim: Cre-dependent reporter lines endogenously express optogenetic effector proteins.
source: Together with Cre-dependent reporter lines that endogenously express optogenetic effector proteins (Madisen et al., 2015; Madisen et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2011), and viral delivery methods (Atasoy et al., 2008; Chatterjee et al., 2018; Deverman et al., 2016; Dimidschstein et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2018; Tervo et al., 2016; Wickersham et al., 2007), these technologies have advanced the precision with which manipulation experiments can be carried out.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing reporter lines and viral methods.

claim: Optogenetic loss-of-function experiments rely on two schemes: 'Direct photoinhibition' and 'ChR-assisted photoinhibition'.
source: Optogenetic loss-of-function experiments rely on two schemes (Wiegert et al., 2017). 'Direct photoinhibition' involves light-gated Cl-/H+ pumps that hyperpolarize neurons (Brown et al., 2018; Chow et al., 2010; Chuong et al., 2014; Han and Boyden, 2007; Zhang et al., 2007) and light-gated Cl- channels that produce hyperpolarization and shunting inhibition (Berndt et al., 2014; Govorunova et al., 2015; Wietek et al., 2014). Direct photoinhibition silences genetically-defined neuronal populations. A second scheme is 'ChR-assisted photoinhibition', which relies on activation of excitatory channelrhodopsins (ChR) expressed in GABAergic neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing optogenetic tools and review.

claim: ChR-assisted photoinhibition has been applied in transgenic mice that express ChR2 in GABAergic neurons; this does not require complex crosses and Cre-mediated expression can be used for other genetic labels.
source: ChR-assisted photoinhibition has been applied in transgenic mice (such as VGAT-ChR2-EYFP) that express ChR2 in GABAergic neurons (Zhao et al., 2011); this does not require complex crosses and Cre-mediated expression can be used for other genetic labels.
evidence: Description of experimental approach supported by citation.

claim: Specific variants of ChR can be targeted to specific GABAergic neurons using interneuron-specific Cre lines.
source: Alternatively, specific variants of ChR (e.g. ChR2 vs. red-shifted variants; Hooks et al., 2015; Klapoetke et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2013) can be targeted to specific GABAergic neurons (e.g. PV vs. Sst neurons) using interneuron-specific Cre lines.
evidence: Description of experimental approach supported by citations.

claim: Both direct photoinhibition and ChR-assisted photoinhibition have been widely used in mice to reveal the involvement of brain areas and neuronal populations in specific phases of behavior.
source: Both direct photoinhibition and ChR-assisted photoinhibition have been widely used in mice to reveal the involvement of brain areas and neuronal populations in specific phases of behavior (Goard et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2014b; Hanks et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Mathis et al., 2017; Morandell and Huber, 2017; Resulaj et al., 2018; Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple behavioral studies using optogenetics.

claim: Neural circuits have local and long-range connections.
source: However, neural circuits have local and long-range connections (Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Hooks et al., 2011; Hooks et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2017; Lefort et al., 2009; Mao et al., 2011; Ozeki et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Strong and nonlinear coupling between neurons, in addition to the photostimulus itself, can affect the spatial and temporal patterns in changes of activity.
source: Strong and nonlinear coupling between neurons, in addition to the photostimulus itself, can affect the spatial and temporal patterns in changes of activity.
evidence: General statement based on understanding of neural circuit properties.

claim: Unexpected effects of optogenetic manipulations are common.
source: As a result, unexpected effects of optogenetic manipulations are common.
evidence: General statement based on review of literature.

claim: Activating and inhibiting Sst+ and PV+ neurons can produce complex and asymmetric effects on excitatory neuron stimulus selectivity in visual cortex and auditory cortex.
source: For example, activating and inhibiting Sst+ and PV+ neurons can produce complex and asymmetric effects on excitatory neuron stimulus selectivity in visual cortex (Adesnik et al., 2012; Atallah et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012) and auditory cortex (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016; Seybold et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effect depends on brain state, nonlinearity, connectivity of the neural circuits, or strength and duration of the light manipulation.
source: The effect depends on brain state (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016), nonlinearity (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016), connectivity of the neural circuits (Seybold et al., 2015), or strength and duration of the light manipulation (Atallah et al., 2014; El-Boustani et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Theoretical studies of networks of excitatory and inhibitory neurons predict counterintuitive responses of neural circuits to perturbations.
source: Theoretical studies of networks of excitatory and inhibitory neurons predict counterintuitive responses of neural circuits to perturbations.
evidence: General statement about theoretical predictions.

claim: Excitation of cortical interneurons can cause a decrease in activity of the same interneurons ('paradoxical effect'), which arises from the interplay between recurrent excitation and inhibition.
source: For example, excitation of cortical interneurons can cause a decrease in activity of the same interneurons ('paradoxical effect'), which arises from the interplay between recurrent excitation and inhibition (Kato et al., 2017; Sanzeni, 2019; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2016; Ozeki et al., 2009; Pehlevan and Sompolinsky, 2014; Rubin et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2017; Tsodyks et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Activity in a brain region can be robust to perturbation of one strongly connected brain region.
source: Activity in a brain region can be robust to perturbation of one strongly connected brain region.
evidence: General statement about circuit properties.

claim: Inactivating one side of anterior lateral motor cortex has little effect on activity in the contralateral hemisphere, despite abundant interhemispheric connections.
source: For example, inactivating one side of anterior lateral motor cortex has little effect on activity in the contralateral hemisphere, despite abundant interhemispheric connections (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Perturbation of other connected brain regions can have dramatic effects.
source: Perturbation of other connected brain regions can have dramatic effects.
evidence: General statement about circuit properties.

claim: Inactivating thalamus causes a rapid and complete collapse of cortical activity.
source: For example, inactivating thalamus causes a rapid and complete collapse of cortical activity (Guo et al., 2017; Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Perturbation experiments using behavior as readout must be interpreted in terms of measured changes in neuronal activity throughout the circuit.
source: Perturbation experiments using behavior as readout must be interpreted in terms of measured changes in neuronal activity throughout the circuit.
evidence: General statement about experimental interpretation.

claim: The direct and indirect effects of circuit manipulations on neuronal activity are rarely measured, particularly in vivo.
source: The direct and indirect effects of circuit manipulations on neuronal activity are rarely measured, particularly in vivo.
evidence: General statement about the state of the field.

claim: Blue light is highly scattered and absorbed by blood.
source: Many light-gated opsins (such as ChR2) are excited by blue light. But blue light is highly scattered and absorbed by blood (Chow et al., 2010; Stujenske et al., 2015; Wiegert et al., 2017; Yizhar et al., 2011; Yona et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of light propagation in tissue.

claim: Red light is less subject to hemoglobin absorption, and thus can propagate further and produces less local heating.
source: Red light is less subject to hemoglobin absorption (Svoboda and Block, 1994), and thus can propagate further and produces less local heating (Liu et al., 2015; Stujenske et al., 2015; Wiegert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of light propagation and heating.

claim: Red-shifted opsins could enable noninvasive manipulations of deep brain regions.
source: Red-shifted opsins (e.g. ReaChR [Lin et al., 2013], Chrimson [Klapoetke et al., 2014], Jaws [Chuong et al., 2014]) could enable noninvasive manipulations of deep brain regions.
evidence: Speculation about potential applications supported by citations to red-shifted opsins.

claim: Direct measurements of light propagation in the intact brain is scarce, and measurements of the distribution of light intensity in vivo are missing.
source: However, direct measurements of light propagation in the intact brain is scarce (Guo et al., 2014b; Ranganathan et al., 2018; Yizhar et al., 2011; Yona et al., 2016), and measurements of the distribution of light intensity in vivo are missing.
evidence: Statement about gaps in the literature supported by citations.

claim: We directly measured the spatial profile of light intensity in cortex at two commonly used wavelengths (blue and orange, 473 and 594 nm) using a photobleaching assay.
source: We directly measured the spatial profile of light intensity in cortex at two commonly used wavelengths (blue and orange, 473 and 594 nm) using a photobleaching assay (Guo et al., 2014b).
evidence: Description of experimental approach used in this study.
